newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: TAX OFFICE DENIES REDUNDANCIES WILL SLOW DOWN RETURNS
The Australian Tax Office has dismissed claims by the Community and Public Sector Union that planned redundancies would delay tax returns.
The CPSU is preparing to launch a major industrial campaign over plans to sack 50 staff, saying it is the beginning of major job cuts by the tax office.
ATO spokesman Bruce Quigley denied CPSU suggestions redundancies would impact on services.
He said the ATO has done its best to minimise forced redundancies.
OPTUS HOPES TO BRING SUPER LEAGUE BACK TO BARGAINING TABLE
Optus says it is disappointed with Super League's decision to withdraw from negotiations on the future of rugby league.
Talks between the Australian Rugby League and Super League over a unified competition broke down yesterday.
Optus chief executive Peter Howell-Davies said he hoped Super League could be persuaded to resume negotiations.
He said he was surprised News Limited has blamed Optus for the collapse of the talks.
Optus said it had no intention of being involved in running rugby league but would continue to assist the ARL in moves to unify the game.
BORBIDGE GOVERNMENT AGAIN RESTS IN LIZ CUNNINGHAM'S HANDS

Queensland's minority government faces another test of its support on the floor of the House when parliament resumes today. The Opposition will move a motion of no-confidence over the aborted multi-million dollar Connolly-Ryan Inquiry into the Criminal Justice Commission.
But the motion is not expected to succeed and attention is already focusing on the Opposition's fallback plan of attack.
The Independent member for Gladstone, Liz Cunningham, will finally reveal her hand when the vote is taken today.
RESEARCHERS HAIL CHEAP SOLAR REVOLUTION
A discovery by researchers at the Australian National University could make solar energy cheap enough to compete with coal-fired power.
Until now, the cost of producing the silicone wafers which make up solar collection panels has made large-scale solar power too expensive to be widely used.
One of the researchers, Dr Andrew Blakers, from ANU's engineering faculty, said the team had come up with a new way of producing the wafers for one-third of their previous costs.
He said they could also produce more efficient solar cells.
